work.framework: 决策时间线与假设追踪
work.scope: Entirely synthetic report exercise: source records, statements and version events are invented. Illustrations are not empirical evidence. No actual study, operational result, market research or participant interview is supplied.

pages.title: Review the decision in its own context.
pages.lead: This report follows five invented version events around a prompt-index decision. The choice is recorded at V3; V4 and V5 are later review entries, not information available at the decision point.
pages.body: The exercise practises separating contemporary information from hindsight. It contains no real governance record, organisational performance or actual approval. Version labels indicate the fictional sequence and must not be presented as real calendar dates.
pages.detail: Separate the supplied synthetic result from your interpretation and any real-world evidence still needed.
pages.question: What information was available when the fictional choice was made?

pages.title: Recover the original question.
pages.lead: The initial question concerns how a reader could identify the current prompt copy. An audit should recover that question before judging a decision against a different goal introduced later.
pages.body: V1 records uncertainty about version visibility and ownership. It does not establish demand for a new platform or a failure of the existing folder. The original problem is narrower than a general claim that the service needs transformation.
pages.detail: Separate the supplied synthetic result from your interpretation and any real-world evidence still needed.

pages.title: Separate knowns and unknowns.
pages.lead: At the decision point, the record distinguishes an available prompt folder from an unconfirmed maintenance role. It supplies no measured user behaviour, cost estimate or implementation agreement.
pages.body: A good audit preserves unknowns rather than filling them with an explanation that seems obvious afterwards. V4 still notes that ownership is unresolved, but that later note must not be misrepresented as a newly discovered fact that was confirmed at V3.
pages.detail: Separate the supplied synthetic result from your interpretation and any real-world evidence still needed.
pages.question: What should remain uncertain even when the later sequence is visible?

pages.title: Keep the considered options.
pages.lead: V2 lists retaining the folder, adding visible version labels or developing a full index. Record alternatives as they were framed rather than replacing them with a more sophisticated option invented later.
pages.body: The lighter-label option aims at the narrow identification question with less proposed structure. The full index has broader ambitions and more maintenance questions. No actual resource availability, usability comparison or feasibility study is supplied for any option.

pages.title: Trace the sequence without hindsight.
pages.lead: V1 frames the question, V2 records options, V3 selects labels for further exploration, V4 preserves the ownership gap and V5 requests a paper walkthrough. The export contains all five entries.
pages.body: Only V1–V3 belong to the recorded decision-time set. The sequence shows how the discussion develops, not that the choice succeeded. It contains one choice event and two follow-up review events after that point.

pages.title: Track an assumption as an assumption.
pages.lead: The V3 reasoning is that a lighter structure may fit the narrow question while maintenance remains unresolved. This is an authored rationale, not evidence that a real team lacked capacity or that labels would work.
pages.body: V4 retains the ownership gap rather than declaring it solved. A traceable audit keeps the assumption, its status and any requested review together. It does not silently upgrade a plausible rationale into an established condition.

pages.title: Distinguish follow-up from outcome.
pages.lead: V5 asks for a paper walkthrough. A request to inspect an option is not an implementation result, user outcome or completion of the proposed work.
pages.body: The dataset supplies no actual walkthrough, publication, adoption or service change. A responsible audit cannot call the decision successful or unsuccessful on an outcome basis. It can only inspect the quality and limits of the recorded reasoning.

pages.title: Check for hindsight bias.
pages.lead: A later reviewer knows that ownership remains unresolved, but should still ask whether that uncertainty was visible and addressed appropriately at the time. Avoid judging an earlier choice as inevitable simply because the full sequence is now available.
pages.body: The audit can compare the stated goal, available information and explicit conditions. It cannot reconstruct private intentions or blame real people from an invented record. Alternative explanations for a reasoning gap should remain questions.

pages.title: Extract a reusable lesson.
pages.lead: A lesson should identify a reasoning practice that could help a future decision, not claim that one fictional option is generally best. Keep the lesson connected to a visible part of the record.
pages.body: For example, preserve the ownership question beside the option choice, and distinguish permission to explore from permission to implement. The lesson concerns documentation discipline; it does not establish a rule that labels are better than indexes.

pages.title: Close the audit with open questions.
pages.lead: Package the original question, option set, decision-time information and later review entries together. Record what remains unknown and what further evidence would support a real outcome review.
pages.body: The five-event source is complete for this exercise. It contains no real dates, appointments, approvals or results. Retain those boundaries when using the report structure for a genuine record, which would require verified context and appropriate access.
